docs.title: i. Regulated industries raise the bar for AI-assisted engineering
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) introduces the Regulated Industry with IBM Bob curriculum for hands-on enablement. [4 min]

Banking and insurance run on software that must satisfy an auditor as well as a user. Each capability has to be explainable. Each rule that governs money has to hold without exception. Each change has to leave a record of what was altered and by whom. These obligations shape how engineering teams in regulated sectors operate. They also define what an AI engineering partner must be able to do before it belongs in the workflow.

This hands-on lab puts IBM Bob to work inside that setting. The application is GFM Bank, a demonstration core-banking system with a FastAPI backend. Role-based access control separates tellers from back-office staff, and a transaction engine enforces overdraft limits and reversal rules. Across three modules you will use Bob to build a documented understanding of that system. You will then generate a production-style teller interface on top of it. Finally you will find and remediate the security vulnerabilities hiding in its code. Each module produces the kind of durable, reviewable artifact a regulated environment expects.

This lab is designed for the IBM sellers, partners, and technical practitioners who demonstrate Bob to clients in regulated sectors. Anyone comfortable with an IDE and a terminal can follow along.

docs.title: ii. What is IBM Bob?
docs.text:
IBM Bob is an AI-powered software engineering partner that supports the entire development lifecycle. Where a traditional code-completion tool is anchored to the moment of writing code, Bob is designed to support the lifecycle around it. In this lab, Bob will:

  • Analyze an unfamiliar codebase and explain its architecture, roles, and business rules
  • Produce reference documentation, requirements, and invariants as persistent files
  • Generate a complete React front-end from a single specification, grounded in local design-system references
  • Diagnose runtime failures from a screenshot and a plain-language description
  • Audit code for security vulnerabilities, remediate them, and verify the result

RECOMMENDED PREREQUISITE: CLIMBING THE AI MATURITY CURVE WITH IBM BOB LEVEL 3

This course is best taken after the Climbing the AI Maturity Curve with IBM Bob Level 3 curriculum. It assumes those concepts are familiar ground: the Agentic Sidebar and its modes, the approval gates that keep the developer in control, and the review-before-trust habit that carried through every stage of that course. The material ahead builds directly upon that foundation.

Bob operates directly within the development environment, so you keep complete visibility into every stage of the process. Bob does the work throughout this lab. Your job is to steer it with prompts and to judge the results before they are trusted.

docs.title: iii. Environment: the GFM Bank demo application
docs.text:
The lab workspace is delivered as a single archive and opened directly in the Bob IDE. It contains four folders, each with a role in the modules ahead.

Folder Responsibility .bob Bob's workspace configuration, with the custom Modes, Skills, and rules pre-configured for this lab bob-banking-lab The GFM Bank demo application codebase and lab assets, including the Python teller_client.py and backoffice_client.py clients carbon-offline-reference Offline copies of IBM Carbon Design System component definitions (TypeScript .d.ts files), which Bob reads to generate accurate, API-correct Carbon code scripts Helper scripts used to set up the lab environment

The GFM Bank backend itself runs remotely on IBM Cloud Code Engine, and the lab's clients and the front-end you build all connect to it over HTTPS. The system exercises the patterns that dominate real banking software:

  • OAuth2 authentication with TELLER and BACKOFFICE roles that differ in their permissions
  • A transfer engine with balance verification, overdraft handling, and a two-transaction debit/credit pattern
  • A data model that relates users and customers to their accounts and transactions
  • An audit trail of what is logged and stored for compliance

Although GFM Bank is a demonstration system, it carries the same invariants and access rules that real core-banking platforms enforce. That is what makes it a credible stage for showing clients how Bob behaves under regulated-industry expectations.

docs.title: iv. The lab journey
docs.text:
AI MATURITY CURVE

The three modules follow the same arc as the previous course. Analyze has Bob build durable understanding of an unfamiliar system and save it into the workspace, which is the persistent-artifact pattern from Module 4 | Scale & Extend. Build is Module 2 | Delegate at project scale: one specification produces a whole application, and an approval gate precedes every consequential step. Secure makes Bob its own reviewer, and the reports it writes are the record a regulated environment requires. The discipline is the one you already practiced, now applied where the stakes are higher.

Module Focus What You'll Do Module 1 - Analyze Understand the application Direct Bob through a read-only analysis of the codebase, then have it produce an architecture document, a data-pipeline analysis, a functional requirements document, and a catalogue of system invariants. Module 2 - Build Generate and iterate Prove the existing teller client against the live backend, generate a complete Carbon-based React teller portal from one specification, then run it and work through the debug loop with screenshots and plain-language prompts. Module 3 - Secure Find and fix Run an OWASP and CWE vulnerability scan, produce a security audit report and a deep dive on the most critical findings, apply the remediations, and verify them.

docs.title: v. What you will build
docs.text:
A WORD ON WORKING WITH GENERATIVE AI

IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most developers are accustomed to. In practice, that means the same prompt can produce different code from one run to the next. This is both a strength and a quirk of the technology, and it is something to work with rather than against.

Precision is what tips the odds in your favor. The more clearly you describe what you want, the more closely Bob's output will mirror your intent; conversely, the smallest change in wording can meaningfully change the generated code. Throughout this lab, your results may differ from the solutions shown — and that is expected, not a defect. Whenever an output diverges, you have three good options: refine the prompt and try again, edit the generated code by hand, or simply proceed if the variation still compiles and runs. Human review remains essential at every step, and never more so than while you are still learning the tool.

The understanding (Module 1 | Analyze). Using Agent mode with read-only tasks, you will have Bob produce four documents:

  • ARCHITECTURE.md
  • DATA_PIPELINE.md
  • FUNCTIONAL_REQUIREMENTS.md
  • An invariants document

Together they describe the system's components and its request lifecycle. They also record every supported business operation and the rules that must never be violated.

The application (Module 2 | Build). Using a single specification, Bob will generate a React teller portal built on the IBM Carbon Design System. It covers login and a dashboard with a live backend status indicator. It also covers the full set of teller operations, from balance inquiry to transfers. You will run it and sign in. You will then resolve the issues that surface with a screenshot and a sentence, reviewing Bob's fix each time.

The assurance (Module 3 | Secure). Bob will scan the codebase for vulnerabilities and rank them by severity. It will document the five most critical with exploit scenarios and secure fixes. It will then apply the remediations and produce a verification report. A final run of the application confirms that the patches broke nothing.

docs.title: vi. Next steps
docs.text: Proceed to the Setup page to download the workspace and sign in to Bob, then continue to Module 1 | Analyze to begin with the codebase analysis.

docs.title: Understanding the Core Banking Codebase
docs.text: MODULE 1 | ANALYZE

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL ANALYZE
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Analyze - Understanding the Core Banking Codebase module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

The discipline of this module is the one you practiced throughout the previous course: understand before changing. Here it applies to a system that handles money. Your control sits in two places. You decide whether to enable auto-approval, and you review each document Bob writes before it is trusted. The documents themselves follow the persistent-artifact pattern of Module 4 | Scale & Extend: understanding captured once and reused by every later conversation.

Before a single line of the GFM Bank application is changed, it must be understood. In this module you direct Bob through a series of read-only analyses of the codebase. Each produces a persistent document in the workspace: first an architecture reference and then a data-pipeline analysis. A functional requirements document and a catalogue of the system's invariants follow. Nothing in the application is modified. What you leave behind is the written understanding that every later module builds upon.

docs.title: ii. WHY THIS MATTERS
docs.text:
In a regulated environment, the questions an auditor asks of a system are the same questions an engineer must answer before changing it. What does each role have permission to do? Which rules govern a transfer, an overdraft, or a fee reversal? What must always remain true in the database, and where in the code is that guaranteed? Answering these by reading source files across a codebase is slow, and the answers rarely get written down.

Bob compresses that discovery work into a handful of prompts. It writes the answers into documents for longevity and maintainability. Those documents serve two purposes at once. They give you the mental model needed for the build work in Module 2. They also form the first entries in the written record that regulated industries require of any system they operate.

docs.title: iii. ANALYZING THE CODEBASE
docs.text: You will send Bob six prompts in sequence. The first four produce the reference documents; the remaining two extract the requirements and the invariants. All of them are read-only tasks.

docs.title: Confirm Agent mode and permissions
docs.text:
1. Before sending any prompts, confirm that Agent mode is selected. Click the mode selector in the bottom-right corner of the Bob panel and choose Agent from the dropdown.

  2. Click the Permissions button at the bottom of the Bob panel. If you wish, enable the Auto-approve toggle so that every permission group is checked:

    • Read
    • Edit
    • Execute
    • MCP
    • Skill
    • Todo
    • Subtask
    • Subagent
    • Mode

    A WORD ON AUTO-APPROVE

    Enabling auto-approval prevents Bob from pausing to ask for manual approval on every individual file read or tool call, which keeps the lab moving. It is a convenience rather than a requirement: if you would rather review Bob's actions individually, leave the toggle unchecked and approve each request as it arrives. You can change the setting at any point in the lab. Either way, the decision about how much autonomy to grant remains yours — the same control you exercised throughout the previous course.

docs.title: Analyze the codebase
docs.text:
1. Paste the following prompt into the Bob chat input. It asks Bob to perform a deep, read-only analysis of the GFM Bank core banking codebase — no code is changed at this stage. Bob reads through the project files and produces a structured explanation along with Mermaid diagrams (a text-based diagramming format used to visualize architectures and data flows.)

    Analyze the GFM Bank Core Banking codebase and provide a comprehensive explanation of its functionality, including:

- **API Architecture**: How the FastAPI backend handles authentication (OAuth2), account management, and transaction processing
- **Role-Based Access Control**: How TELLER and BACKOFFICE roles differ in their permissions and capabilities
- **Transaction Processing**: The transfer logic including balance verification, overdraft handling, and the two-transaction debit/credit pattern
- **Data Model**: The relationship between users, customers, accounts, and transactions tables
- **Client Applications**: How teller_client.py and backoffice_client.py interact with the API

Additionally, create detailed Mermaid diagrams showing:

- System architecture with all components
- API endpoint structure and authentication flow
- Transaction processing sequence
- Data model relationships

Clearly state key invariants, business rules, and assumptions made by the code.
    • After pasting, the prompt collapses in the chat input into a grey pill labelled "Pasted text #1 - xx lines".
    • In this example it pasted as 16 lines; formatting differences may give you a different count, which is fine as long as the prompt itself is intact.
    • You can click the pill to expand and review the full prompt before sending.

  2. Click the "Pasted text #1 - xx lines" pill to open a popup showing the full prompt.

    • Verify that the pasted content matches the prompt above, then click Save to close the popup and return to the chat input.
    • This review step ensures you send exactly the instructions you intend.

  3. Click the Send button (the arrow icon in the bottom-right corner of the chat input) or hit Enter to submit the prompt.

  4. Bob begins working immediately. Because this prompt involves only read-only actions, little or no manual approval should be needed. Bob reads through the project directory and produces a structured explanation; you can watch its progress in the panel as it works through each file.

  5. When the analysis is complete, take a few minutes to read through Bob's response.

    • This is where your mental model of the GFM Bank application forms, before anything is changed in the modules ahead.
    • It covers the architecture and the roles. It also covers the transaction logic and the data relationships.

  6. Scroll down through the response to read the complete analysis. It includes the Mermaid diagrams Bob generated: one for the system architecture and one for the API flow, followed by the transaction sequences and the data model relationships.

docs.title: Produce the architecture document
docs.text:
1. Now ask Bob to turn its analysis into a permanent architectural reference. Paste the following prompt into the chat input:

    Based on your analysis, create a comprehensive ARCHITECTURE.md document that includes:

 1. **Executive Summary**: One-paragraph overview of the system
 2. **System Architecture**: High-level Mermaid diagram showing all components
 3. **Component Descriptions**: Detailed explanation of each module
 4. **API Reference**: All endpoints with their purposes and access controls
 5. **Data Model**: Entity-relationship diagram using Mermaid
 6. **Transaction Flow**: Sequence diagram for key operations (transfer, balance inquiry)
 7. **Security Model**: Authentication, authorization, and data protection
 8. **Functional Requirements**: List of supported business operations
 9. **Non-Functional Requirements**: Performance, reliability, and scalability considerations
 10. **Assumptions and Constraints**: Technical and business limitations

Save this as ARCHITECTURE.md in the current directory.

  2. As before, you can click the "Pasted text #1 - xx lines" pill to expand and verify the full prompt.

    • From this point on, the pasted-text pill will not be shown again for every prompt, but the process is always the same.
    • Click the pill and review the content, then press Save to confirm.

  3. Click Save to close the popup and return to the chat input, then hit Enter to submit the prompt.

  4. Bob begins writing the ARCHITECTURE.md file.

    • This task involves writing a new file, so Bob uses its edit tools to create the document directly in the project directory.
    • Watch the panel for progress updates as it works through each section.

  5. Bob confirms that it has created the document. Click ARCHITECTURE.md in the file explorer sidebar to open it.

  6. Review the contents. Bob has produced a structured reference document covering all of the sections you specified, from the executive summary through to the assumptions and constraints.

docs.title: Analyze the data pipeline
docs.text:
1. Now ask Bob for a deeper analysis of the transaction processing pipeline. Paste the following prompt into the chat input:

    Create a detailed data pipeline analysis that covers:

- **Request Lifecycle**: From HTTP request to database commit
- **Transaction States**: How transfers move through validation, execution, and confirmation
- **Error Handling**: What happens when transactions fail at each stage
- **Consistency Guarantees**: How the system ensures ACID properties
- **Audit Trail**: What information is logged and stored for compliance

Include a Mermaid flowchart showing the complete data pipeline from client request to persisted transaction.

    This prompt is shorter, so it is sent directly rather than collapsed into a pasted-text pill.

  2. Click the Send button (or hit Enter on your keyboard) to submit the data pipeline analysis prompt.

  3. Bob begins working on the analysis. Watch the Agentic Sidebar as it reads through the project files and constructs the flowchart and supporting documentation.

  4. When complete, Bob confirms it has written DATA_PIPELINE.md to the project directory. Read through the summary in the panel to see what was documented.

  5. Click DATA_PIPELINE.md in the file explorer sidebar to open the document.

  6. When working with Markdown documents in the Bob IDE, right-click the file tab and select Open Preview (keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+V) to render the formatting. Headers, tables, and code blocks are far easier to read this way than in the raw source view.

  7. The document is now displayed in formatted preview mode. Headings and bullet points render cleanly, and so do the tables.

  8. Scroll through the document to review all five sections Bob produced, including the Mermaid flowchart at the end showing the full data pipeline from HTTP request to committed transaction.

  9. Although the IDE editor does not render Mermaid diagrams by default, Bob's chat panel can display them visually. Send the following prompt to render the diagram directly in the sidebar:

    Render the Mermaid diagram visually in the IBM Bob chat window.

  10. Bob renders the Mermaid flowchart as a visual diagram inside the chat panel. You can now read the complete data pipeline without needing a separate extension.

  11. Click the rendered diagram to open it in the main editor window at full size, where you can zoom in and explore the pipeline stages in detail.

docs.title: Extract the functional requirements
docs.text:
1. Next, paste the following prompt into the chat input and hit Enter to have Bob extract and document every functional requirement from the codebase:

    Extract and document all functional requirements from the codebase:

- **Teller Operations**:

   - What can a teller do?
   - What information can they access?
   - What are the limitations?

- **Back-Office Operations**:

   - What administrative functions are available?
   - What privileged operations require BACKOFFICE role?

- **Business Rules**:

   - Overdraft limits and enforcement
   - Transfer validation rules
   - Fee reversal constraints

Format this as a structured requirements document with clear acceptance criteria.

  2. Bob begins working. Watch the Agentic Sidebar as it reads through the source files and builds the structured requirements document.

  3. Bob continues through the codebase, reading additional files to ensure all functional requirements are captured.

  4. Bob completes the task and confirms that FUNCTIONAL_REQUIREMENTS.md has been created in the project directory.

  5. The file explorer sidebar now shows FUNCTIONAL_REQUIREMENTS.md. Click the file to open it.

  6. Right-click the file tab and select Open Preview to view the formatted document with all sections rendered.

  7. Review the functional requirements document. It lists every supported operation — teller and back-office — along with the business rules that govern them.

docs.title: Document the invariants
docs.text:
1. Paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar and hit Enter to have Bob identify and document all system invariants and assumptions:

    Identify and document all system invariants and assumptions:

- **Data Invariants**: Rules that must always hold true in the database
- **Business Invariants**: Financial rules that cannot be violated
- **Security Invariants**: Access control rules that must be enforced
- **Technical Assumptions**: What the code assumes about its environment

For each invariant, explain:

- What the invariant is
- Where in the code it's enforced
- What could go wrong if violated

  2. Bob starts reading through the codebase to identify and document the invariants and assumptions.

  3. Bob continues reading files and extracting invariant rules as it works through the codebase.

  4. Bob completes the analysis and confirms that the invariants file has been written. Read through Bob's summary in the Agentic Sidebar to review its findings.

  5. Right-click the INVARIANTS.md file (or similarly named file) in the explorer sidebar and select Open Preview (Ctrl+Shift+V) to view the formatted document.

  6. Review the invariants document. Bob has catalogued every invariant it found in the codebase — data and business invariants as well as security and technical ones. For each, it records where the code enforces it and what would break if it were violated.

docs.title: iv. KEY TAKEAWAYS
docs.text:
• Read-only analysis in Agent mode lets Bob explain an unfamiliar codebase without touching it.
  • Asking for documents rather than answers turns a conversation into persistent artifacts that later modules and later teammates can build upon.
  • The pasted-text pill is a review gate: expand it, confirm the prompt is intact, then send.
  • In a regulated setting, the invariants document is the most consequential of the four. It states what must always hold and where the code enforces it (and also states what breaks if a rule is violated.)
  • File names and the location of findings vary from run to run; what matters is that each analysis is complete and reviewed.

With the application understood and documented, the next module transitions from reading to building. In Module 2 | Build, you will prove the existing teller client against the live GFM Bank backend, then have Bob generate a complete Carbon-based teller portal from a single specification.

docs.title: Building the Carbon Teller Front-End
docs.text: MODULE 2 | BUILD

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL BUILD
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Build - Building the Carbon Teller Front-End module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

This chapter is Module 2 | Delegate at project scale. One specification produces an entire application, and an approval gate precedes every consequential step. The specification also grounds Bob deliberately. It requires that every Carbon prop name and token come from the local .d.ts files rather than from memory, which is the context-quality discipline of Module 4 | Scale & Extend applied to a design system. The result is code that maps onto the real backend and the real component library.

The previous module left you with a documented understanding of GFM Bank. This module puts it to use. You first prove that the existing Python teller client can reach the live GFM Bank backend and return a real account balance. You then hand Bob a single, detailed specification and have it generate a complete React teller portal on the IBM Carbon Design System, grounded in the offline Carbon references shipped with the workspace. By the end of the chapter the portal is built and its dependencies are installed with a clean compile.

docs.title: ii. WHY THIS MATTERS
docs.text:
A front-end for a regulated system has two obligations that ordinary web applications can afford to relax.

  1. It must call the real backend, with its real endpoints and roles and validation rules. A teller interface that drifts from the core banking API is a compliance problem in its own right.
  2. It must also present a consistent, accessible interface that an institution can standardize on, which is why the specification insists on the IBM Carbon Design System.

Both obligations are met the same way: by grounding Bob in authoritative local sources before it writes a line of code. The Python clients from Module 1 describe the API as it actually is. The carbon-offline-reference folder describes the component library as it actually is. The specification directs Bob to read both, and the build you observe in this chapter is the consequence.

docs.title: iii. PROVING THE BACKEND CONNECTION
docs.text:
ATTENTION: NON-DETERMINISTIC WORK AHEAD

The sequence of commands and approvals in this section is specific to the run captured in the screenshots, which was performed on Windows with PowerShell. Depending on your operating system and Bob version, the issues you encounter will differ, and you may encounter none at all. In every case Bob works toward a viable alternative on its own. Where it does not, a plain-language description of the problem is enough to move it forward. Later chapters demonstrate this.

Before building anything new, confirm that the existing teller client can reach the live backend. The exchange also shows how Bob works through environment-specific failures on its own.

docs.title: Start a new task and send the test prompt
docs.text:
1. Open a new chat window by clicking the + button.

  2. Paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar chat input and hit Enter to test the teller client against the live backend server:

    Can you test my teller client with my server:
https://wxo-corebanking-backend.1944johjccn7.eu-de.codeengine.appdomain.cloud/docs

Use IBAN DE89545769475769453536 to check the balance
    CONNECTIVITY ISSUES?

    The database and transactions supporting the wxo-corebanking-backend server resets every 60 minutes to its default stage to ensure that the environment is properly maintained. Resets to the server take approximately 1 minute to resolve. If you are experiencing connectivity issues, wait a few minutes and try again. If it continues to fail, reach out to the documentation authors for support.

  3. Bob starts working, reading the teller client code and connecting to the backend server to run the balance inquiry.

docs.title: Work through the approval loop
docs.text:
1. Bob requests permission to run an Execute Command that sets the COREBANK_URL environment variable and runs the teller client script against the live backend. Click Approve for task to allow it.

  2. In this example, the first command failed (exit code 1) because a trailing space in the URL caused set to encode it as %20.

    • Bob explains the issue and requests permission to retry with a corrected PowerShell command that runs python teller_client.py directly from the code directory.
    • Click Approve for task.

  3. The second attempt also failed (exit code 1): the cd path was not resolving correctly.

    • Bob now requests permission to run python directly with the full path to teller_client.py from the workspace root.
    • Click Approve for task.

  4. The previous runs defaulted to localhost because the environment variable was not being passed through correctly.

    • Bob requests permission to run a PowerShell command that sets $env:COREBANK_URL inline before calling python teller_client.py, so that the remote URL is picked up.
    • Click Approve for task.

  5. That command failed because the backend server took longer than 10 seconds to respond.

    • Bob reports that DNS resolved and the TLS handshake completed — the server is simply slow to start — and requests permission to retry with a 90-second timeout.
    • Click Approve.

  6. Bob now requests permission to run a PowerShell command that sets $env:COREBANK_URL inline and runs the teller client with a TIMEOUT = 60 override, giving the cold-starting backend more time to respond. Click Approve for task.

  7. After several failed attempts, Bob has sought out an alternative on its own: it has written a _test_teller.py helper script to isolate the connection test and requests permission to run python _test_teller.py with a timeout_seconds: 180 override. Click Approve for task.

  8. The helper script ran successfully and returned live transaction data from the backend — multiple PAYMENT records with account IDs, timestamps, and EUR amounts.

    • Bob confirms that everything works and requests permission to delete the temporary file (del _test_teller.py).
    • Click Approve for task to let it clean up.

  9. Bob deletes the temporary file and delivers the result: the teller client connected successfully.

    • It displays the summary for IBAN DE89545769475769453536: the account ID and customer ID, together with a current balance of €5,581.33.
    • Below them are the latest five ledger rows with booking timestamps and EUR amounts.
    • Record that balance to a notepad, as you will meet it again at the end of the next chapter.

docs.title: iv. GENERATING THE TELLER PORTAL
docs.text: With the backend proven reachable, hand Bob the specification for the front-end. It is a long prompt by design. It names the backend and the credentials. It lists every teller operation to replicate and the Carbon components to use. It also sets out the technical and security requirements to honor.

docs.title: Start a fresh task
docs.text:
1. In the Bob IDE, locate the IBM BOB panel on the right side of the screen.

    • Click the New Task button (the + icon in the top-right corner of the panel) to open a fresh task session.
    • A new task gives Bob a clean context window, free from the previous conversation.

  2. Before submitting the prompt, confirm once again that Bob is set to Agent mode; the Agent toggle is visible at the bottom-left of the panel. If you are comfortable with it, confirm that the Auto-approve permissions are enabled as well.

docs.title: Send the specification
docs.text:
1. Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar. It instructs Bob to build a comprehensive React-based teller front-end for GFM Bank using the IBM Carbon Design System, referencing the local Carbon component .d.ts files for accurate API shapes:

    Before beginning implementation, read carbon-offline-reference/CARBON_REFERENCE.md to locate the .d.ts path for every Carbon component you plan to use, then read each of those .d.ts files. All prop names, valid values, design token names, and icon names must come from those local files — do not use memory or any external source for Carbon API shapes.

Create a comprehensive React-based Teller Front-End application for GFM Bank using IBM Carbon Design System with the following specifications:

Application Requirements:
- Develop a modern, professional banking teller interface that connects to the Core Banking backend server at https://wxo-corebanking-backend.1944johjccn7.eu-de.codeengine.appdomain.cloud/docs

Authentication System:
- Implement a secure login page with IBM Carbon form components
- Store credentials in environment variables (.env file): username "teller" and password "teller123"
- Include proper form validation and error handling
- Add session management with secure token storage

Main Dashboard Layout:
- Display "GFM Bank" branding prominently in the header using IBM Carbon design tokens
- Position a real-time backend server status indicator in the top-right corner showing "Online" (green) or "Offline" (red/gray) with automatic health check polling
- Implement IBM Carbon's UI Shell component for consistent navigation and layout

Teller Operations Interface:
- Replicate all functionality from the teller_client.py with modern UI components:

- Account balance inquiry with IBAN input and formatted currency display
- Customer account creation form with validation
- Money deposit interface with amount input and transaction confirmation
- Money withdrawal interface with balance verification
- Account-to-account transfer with dual IBAN inputs and amount specification
- Transaction history viewer with sortable, filterable data tables
- Account details lookup with comprehensive information display

Design Considerations:
- Before writing any code, read carbon-offline-reference/CARBON_REFERENCE.md and the .d.ts file for every component you intend to use. Use only prop names and values found in those files. Do not rely on memory for any Carbon prop shape.
- Apply IBM Carbon banking theme with professional color palette (blues, grays, whites).
- Use only token names listed in the Design Token Quick-Reference table in CARBON_REFERENCE.md — written as var(--cds-) in CSS. Never use removed v10 token names (brand-01, ui-01, ui-02) or the bx-- CSS prefix.

- Use Carbon's data table components for transaction lists and account information
- Implement Carbon notifications for success/error messages
- Add loading states using Carbon skeleton components during API calls
- Ensure responsive design for various screen sizes
- Include proper error boundaries and fallback UI
- Add confirmation modals for critical operations (withdrawals, transfers)
- Display currency amounts with proper formatting (EUR symbol, decimal places)
- Implement form validation with real-time feedback
- Add accessibility features (ARIA labels, keyboard navigation)

Technical Implementation:
- Use React functional components with hooks
- Implement Axios or Fetch for API communication
- Add environment variable configuration for backend URL and credentials
- Add a "proxy" field in package.json pointing to the backend URL so the dev server forwards API requests and avoids CORS errors in the browser
- Include proper TypeScript types or PropTypes validation
- Structure components logically (pages, components, services, utils)
- Implement React Router for navigation between views
- Add state management (Context API or Redux) for user session and app state
- Include automated backend health checks with configurable intervals
- Handle API errors gracefully with user-friendly messages

Security Features:
- Implement JWT token handling if applicable
- Add automatic logout on session expiration
- Sanitize all user inputs
- Use HTTPS for all API communications
- Implement CORS handling via the dev server proxy — do not hardcode the backend URL as the axios baseURL in development

Additional Features:
- Add a dashboard summary showing key metrics
- Include quick action buttons for common teller operations
- Implement search functionality for customer accounts
- Add print receipt functionality for transactions
- Include audit trail logging for compliance

Provide complete, production-ready code with proper project structure, package.json with all dependencies (react, @carbon/react, react-router-dom, axios, dotenv), and clear setup instructions.

  2. With the prompt pasted into the Agentic Sidebar, hit Enter to execute the instructions.

docs.title: Watch Bob ground itself in the Carbon references
docs.text:
1. Bob begins working immediately. As instructed, it first reads carbon-offline-reference/CARBON_REFERENCE.md. It then expands to read the individual Carbon component .d.ts files. These are TypeScript declaration files that describe each component's exact props and API surface. Among the components it reads are SideNavLink and Header, then SideNav and HeaderName, along with DataTable and others. This reading phase is what allows Bob to generate accurate component code rather than inventing prop names from memory.

  2. Having finished reading the Carbon .d.ts files, Bob announces that it has everything it needs and moves on to understand the workspace layout. It lists files in bob-banking-lab and in bob-banking-lab/LABs, and then in the Banking Industry folder.

  3. Bob continues working through its plan. It has listed the full bob-banking-lab/LABs directory tree, read the existing Teller Application lab files, and is reading teller_client.py to understand every API endpoint the new front-end will need to call.

  4. Bob has finished its discovery phase and produced a complete map of the GFM Bank backend API. The Agentic Sidebar lists every endpoint it found by reading the Python client files:

    • POST /token (login)
    • GET /accounts
    • GET /transactions/{account_id}
    • POST /transfer
    • GET /customers
    • POST /transactions/{account_id} (deposit and reversal)
    • PATCH /accounts/{account_id}/overdraft

    This discovery step is what ensures the generated front-end maps exactly onto the real backend rather than onto a generic template that would need manual correction.

docs.title: Approve the build steps
docs.text:
1. Bob reaches its first approval checkpoint. After declaring that it is ready to build, it attempted to write teller-ui/package.json, but the target directory did not yet exist.

    • Bob now requests permission to run a shell command to create the folder.
    • Click Approve for task to allow Bob to create the directory and continue.

  2. Progress is visible: the mkdir command ran, package.json was written, and two additional files were edited. Note the green change indicator on bob-banking-lab in the file explorer — Bob is actively writing files to your workspace. Bob has also encountered a limitation: creating the public/ sub-directory failed because the file-write tool cannot handle spaces in deeply nested folder paths.

    • Bob self-corrects and requests permission to run a cd command to navigate into the new directory before creating sub-directories.
    • In the Tools awaiting approval panel, click Approve for task.

  3. The first cd command has run, and a second Execute Command approval is waiting for another cd deeper into the project structure. Click Approve for task again.

  4. Bob requests permission to write public/index.html using a PowerShell Set-Content command, to avoid path-handling issues with special characters and spaces.

    • The Tools awaiting approval panel shows the request, containing the complete HTML boilerplate for the GFM Bank Teller Portal.
    • Click Approve for task.

  5. That command exited with code 1 because of PowerShell quote-escaping syntax.

    • Bob immediately self-corrects and formulates a refined PowerShell script that uses a $content variable to write public/index.html safely.
    • Click Approve for task.

  6. To handle workspace paths with spaces and special characters reliably across platforms, Bob switches to a Python script using pathlib. The script creates every target sub-directory and writes public/index.html. The sub-directories are:

    • public
    • src
    • src/pages
    • src/components
    • src/context
    • src/services
    • src/utils

    Click Approve for task to run it.

  7. After the directory-creation script executes, Bob runs a verification script using BASE.iterdir() to confirm that the target directory and sub-directories exist before proceeding. Click Approve for task.

  8. Bob determines that writing a dedicated Python script file and executing it will be the cleanest way to generate the remaining application code across the folder hierarchy. The Agentic Sidebar shows it changing approach: "Let me try a different approach — write a Python script file first and then execute it."

  9. Bob pauses to inspect the current state of the project folder with a dir command before running its generator. Click Approve for task.

  10. The directory check succeeds. Bob confirms that the target directories exist and begins writing a Python generator script designed to produce all of the application's source files at once.

  11. Bob has written scripts/generate_teller_ui.py and requests permission to execute it with python scripts/generate_teller_ui.py.

    • Because running a newly generated script triggers a security confirmation, a Security warning notice appears.
    • Tick the I understand the risk checkbox, then click Approve to run the script and generate the complete front-end codebase.

  12. With the generator script approved and running, Bob scaffolds the full set of application components and service layers.

  13. Bob has generated all source files, verified them, and written the project README.md.

    • Bob now begins final validation by preparing to run npm install inside the new UI directory to ensure all dependencies resolve cleanly.
    • In the Tools awaiting approval panel, click Approve for task.

  14. With all npm packages installed, Bob is ready for the final build check, which verifies that the React code compiles with no TypeScript or syntax errors. Click Approve for task to run the build.

docs.title: Review what was built
docs.text:
1. The task is complete. The top of the Agentic Sidebar displays a green All tasks completed! badge with the sub-task counter, confirming that every planned step finished. Below it, Bob presents a What was built summary with a File map table listing each generated file alongside its purpose. Key files include:

    • package.json — the dependencies and the proxy to the backend URL
    • .env — the teller credentials via REACT_APP_TELLER_USERNAME and REACT_APP_TELLER_PASSWORD
    • src/index.scss — Carbon imports and custom CSS variable overrides
    • src/services/api.js — an Axios instance with a Bearer-token interceptor and auto-logout on 401
    • src/context/AuthContext.js — session state via sessionStorage with login() and logout()

    The teller front-end has been generated from a single prompt. It is mapped onto the real backend and built against the real Carbon library.

docs.title: v. KEY TAKEAWAYS
docs.text:
• Prove the backend before building on it: the teller client's successful balance inquiry establishes the ground truth the front-end must reproduce.
  • Environment-specific failures are normal in agentic work, and Bob works through them by explaining each one and proposing an alternative; your role is to read the explanation before approving.
  • A long, explicit specification is what makes a one-prompt build reliable. It names the backend and the operations, then the components and the constraints, so that Bob is not left to guess.
  • Grounding Bob in local references (the Python clients and the Carbon .d.ts files) produces code that matches the real API and the real component library.
  • Security warnings on newly generated scripts are gates you clear deliberately, after reading what the script will do.
  • The build ends with a file map and a clean compile. From there the application is yours to run and to judge.

The application is built, but has not yet been run. In Running, Debugging, and Iterating, you start the development server and sign in. You then work through the issues that surface with a screenshot and a sentence, reviewing Bob's fix each time, before completing the module's teller task.

docs.title: Running, Debugging, and Iterating
docs.text: MODULE 2 | BUILD

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL DO
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Build - Running, Debugging, and Iterating module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

Every fix in this chapter begins with evidence — a screenshot of the failing screen — and ends with your review of Bob's summary before the server restarts. Between those two points Bob works on its own. It diagnoses the problem and probes the backend with curl. It then edits the code and rebuilds. This is the discipline of the previous course applied to a live application. The investigation is delegated; the result is verified before it is trusted; the restart stays in your hands.

A generated application is a starting point rather than a finished product. This chapter closes the gap.

You start the teller portal Bob built and sign in. You then resolve the issues that surface: a login that fails, a page that looks plainer than the specification asked for, and a dashboard whose counters read zero. The method is the same every time:

  1. Take a screenshot and describe the problem in a sentence.
  2. Review what Bob changes before you restart.

The chapter closes with the module's teller task, retrieving the balance for a specific IBAN through the portal you built.

docs.title: ii. WHY THIS MATTERS
docs.text:
Generative AI produces a working application far faster than a team could write one. It also produces one with defects, because no specification can anticipate every runtime detail. A proxy behaves unexpectedly, a credential differs from what was assumed, or a token arrives late. The skill that matters in practice is the iteration loop, and it is a skill clients ask about directly: how does a practitioner fix what the agent got wrong without becoming an expert in the generated code?

The answer this chapter demonstrates requires no reading of the source. A screenshot supplies the visual context and a plain-language sentence supplies the intent. Bob investigates from there. It reads its own code and tests the backend, then applies a fix that it explains. In a regulated industry setting, that explanation matters as much as the fix itself: each iteration leaves a record of what was wrong and what changed.

docs.title: iii. STARTING THE APPLICATION
docs.text: Bob's completion message from the previous chapter ends with the terminal commands needed to start the application. Your task for this module is to start the portal, sign in, and find the latest transactions for the client with IBAN DE89545769475769453536.

docs.title: Start the development server
docs.text:
1. Scroll through Bob's final message until you find the terminal commands needed to start the front-end.

  2. Click Terminal in the top menu bar to open the terminal panel in the IDE.

  3. Click New Terminal to open a fresh terminal session in the project directory.

  4. Paste and execute the first terminal command Bob provided, for example:

    cd gfm-teller-app

    Your exact commands may differ depending on how Bob named the project directory.

  5. Paste and execute the next command Bob provided, typically the dependency install:

    npm install

  6. Paste and execute the final startup command Bob provided, typically:

    npm start

  7. Review the output for the URL where your application is running. In most cases this is localhost:3000.

  8. Navigate to the URL in your browser. The page may display a blank white screen for one to two minutes while the React application compiles and loads. This is normal; wait for it to finish before advancing along the lab steps.

docs.title: Find the credentials and sign in
docs.text:
1. The GFM Bank — Teller Portal login screen appears and asks for credentials. Return to the Bob chat panel to find out where they are stored.

  2. Review Bob's completion message and look for a line mentioning login credentials. Bob may paste them directly in the chat or, as in this case, indicate that they are stored in an .env file in the project directory.

  3. Navigate to gfm-teller-app/.env in the file explorer sidebar.

  4. Open .env. It contains the REACT_APP_TELLER_USERNAME and REACT_APP_TELLER_PASSWORD values Bob configured during the build; these are the credentials for the application.

  5. Enter the username and password from .env into the login form and click Sign in. If you cannot locate the credentials, review Bob's output or check .env. You can also simply ask Bob for them.

YOUR APPLICATION MAY LOOK DIFFERENT

Because Bob is generative, your portal may look quite different from the screenshots in this chapter. The following examples show alternative renderings of the login page, the dashboard, and the balance inquiry page from other runs of the same specification.

docs.title: iv. THE DEBUG LOOP
docs.text: In the run captured here, two issues appear at once: the login attempt fails with a network error, and the login page looks plain despite the specification's instruction to use Carbon components. Both get fixed, starting with the login. You may or may not experience these issues; if your portal works, skip ahead to the next section.

docs.title: Fix the login error and the plain design
docs.text:
1. When you encounter an error or want a UI improvement, the process is always the same.

    • Take a screenshot of the problem and paste it into Bob's Agentic Sidebar chat, then hit Enter to execute.
    • Be sure to describe the issue in natural, plain language (as if you were describing the problem to a colleague.)
    • Start by taking a screenshot of the entire page showing the login error.

  2. The screenshot captures both the network error and the plain design.

  3. Paste the screenshot directly into the Bob chat input so that Bob has visual context for what is going wrong.

  4. Alongside the screenshot, describe the issue in plain language — for example: "The login is failing with a network error, and the page design looks plain. Please fix both." No knowledge of the root cause is required; Bob reads the code, investigates, and resolves the issue on its own.

  5. Bob has already diagnosed the root cause.

    • The network error is a CORS issue: the login function calls the backend with the absolute BASE_URL through a bare axios.post, bypassing the dev-server proxy entirely. Bob requests permission to run a curl -s -X POST command against the backend to verify the actual API response.
    • Click Approve for task.

  6. The first curl command has run.

    • Bob now requests permission to run a second curl -si -X POST against the backend's /token endpoint with a different Authorization header, probing for the correct credentials.
    • Click Approve for task.

  7. The curl test confirmed that teller1/password1 returns Bad credentials from the backend.

    • Bob requests permission to run another curl -si against /token with a different header to discover the correct credentials.
    • Click Approve for task.

  8. Bob requests permission for one further curl -s -X POST against the /token endpoint. Click Approve for task.

  9. Bob has confirmed that the real credentials are teller / teller123.

    • It outlines a two-part fix: switch to relative URLs and update .env, then redesign the login header.
    • It updates .env with the correct credentials and begins reading LoginPage.js for the redesign.

  10. Bob has rewritten LoginPage.js with a Carbon-styled header and applied the matching SCSS changes.

    • It requests permission to run cd gfm-teller-app && npx react-scripts build 2>&1 to confirm that the updated application compiles cleanly.
    • Click Approve for task.

  11. The fix is complete.

    • Bob's message confirms the new credentials to use: username teller and password teller123.
    • A server restart is required for the changes to take effect.

docs.title: Restart the server and test the fix
docs.text:
1. Click Terminal.

  2. Click New Terminal.

  3. In the terminal sidebar list, find the previously opened terminal labelled node — the terminal where the app is running — and click it to switch to that session. If you closed that terminal, simply run the same startup commands again.

  4. Identify the terminal where the application process is currently running; it shows active output from npm start or node.

  5. Press Ctrl+C in the running terminal to stop the development server. The prompt returns and accepts input again.

  6. Type npm start (or the startup command Bob originally provided) and press Enter to restart the application with the credential changes applied.

  7. Return to your browser and refresh the app URL. The page will remain on a white loading screen for a minute or more while the React build recompiles, which is expected.

  8. The app loads.

    A BROWSER WARNING YOU CAN DISMISS

    Some browsers warn that the password has appeared in a known data breach. This is expected, because the lab uses the simple demo credentials teller and teller123. The application runs locally and holds no real sensitive data. Close the warning and proceed.

  9. The login page design has been improved by Bob's fix: the Carbon components are styled correctly and the page now looks the part.

  10. Enter the new credentials (teller / teller123) and click Sign in.

  11. The design is fixed, but a network error still appears on sign-in. This needs a separate investigation.

docs.title: Resolve the remaining network error
docs.text:
1. Take a screenshot of the page showing the network error, following the same process as before.

  2. Paste the screenshot into the Bob chat alongside a brief description of the problem, then hit Enter to execute.

  3. Bob investigates the network error, reading the API service files and environment configuration to find the root cause.

  4. Bob discovers that its previous fix to api.js was not persisted: the login() function still calls axios.post(${BASE_URL}/token, ...) directly, bypassing the dev-server proxy.

    • Bob has rewritten gfm-teller-app/src/services/api.js with a complete fix and requests permission to run cd gfm-teller-app && npx react-scripts build to confirm that the build still passes.
    • Click Approve for task.

  5. Bob requests permission to run cd gfm-teller-app && findstr /n "BASE_URL" to scan api.js for any remaining absolute BASE_URL references, confirming that the rewrite removed every direct backend call that bypassed the proxy. Click Approve for task.

  6. Bob confirms that the fix is complete. Review its summary to understand what changed.

  7. Another restart is required to apply this fix.

    • Depending on the nature of a fix, a restart may not be needed (sometimes a page refresh is enough), so review Bob's instructions each time.
    • As before, press Ctrl+C in the running terminal to stop the application.

  8. Type npm start and press Enter to restart the application.

  9. Enter the credentials and click Sign in again to test whether the network error is resolved.

  10. Sign-in succeeds and you reach the main dashboard. Two further issues are visible, however. The dashboard design still needs work. The Accounts counter reads zero, and so do the Customers and Balances counters.

docs.title: Improve the dashboard
docs.text:
1. As before, take a screenshot of the dashboard showing the design you want Bob to improve.

  2. Paste the screenshot and type a plain-language prompt into the chat input.

    • For example: "Great, I can sign in now! Finally, lets add some nicer aesthetics to the teller portal, like you did for the login page."
    • When ready, hit Enter to execute.

  3. Bob responds with a plan for the visual uplift that sets out six goals, and then begins working. The goals cover the header and the side navigation. They also cover the page header and the metric tiles, followed by the quick-action tiles and the global spacing.

  4. Bob begins the visual improvements. Watch the terminal panel as the dev server at localhost:3000 automatically recompiles with the updated styles.

  5. Bob has verified the auth token flow and read index.scss to plan the uplift.

    • Bob requests permission to run a type command to read a temporary file as part of its CSS planning.
    • Click Approve for task.

  6. Bob has confirmed that the "teller" token is a bare string accepted as Bearer auth and has read the current index.scss.

    • Bob requests permission to run another curl -s against the backend to verify the token handling further before applying the visual changes.
    • Click Approve for task.

  7. Click Approve to allow Bob to proceed with the next change.

  8. Bob confirms that the API works with Bearer teller and that the "Forbidden" errors are a token-timing issue: the dashboard loads before the token propagates. It notes this as minor and continues planning before starting the visual work.

  9. Bob works through the remaining component updates.

  10. Bob has written the updated index.scss, AppShell.js, and DashboardPage.js with the full visual uplift. That covers a branded header and richer metric tiles.

    • Bob also adds quick-action cards and a token-timing fix.
    • It requests permission to run a Node.js command that verifies the new Carbon icons exist before triggering the build.
    • Click Approve for task.

  11. Bob has confirmed that all three required Carbon icons exist and requests permission to run cd gfm-teller-app && npx react-scripts build with a 300-second timeout to produce the final build with the visual changes applied. Click Approve for task.

  12. Bob's task is complete. The chat panel summarizes every change applied. There are quick-action tiles and section headings, along with a header carrying the BankMark SVG. The "Forbidden" fix in DashboardPage.js is listed as well. The dev server has already recompiled.

  13. Return to your browser, reload the app URL, and sign in again to see the updated design.

docs.title: Fix the empty dashboard counters
docs.text:
1. Before the module's final task, address the remaining issue: the Accounts counter reads zero, and so do the Customers and Combined Balances counters.

    • A "Dashboard load failed — Forbidden" toast is also visible in the top-right corner.
    • The dashboard is not fetching its summary data from the backend correctly.

  2. As before, write a prompt describing the issue and attach a screenshot for context. Then hit Enter to execute.

  3. Bob identifies the zeros as an API response-shape mismatch and requests permission to run a curl -s command against the backend to determine the exact response structure before writing any fix. Click Approve for task.

  4. Tick I understand the risk and click Approve.

  5. Click Approve.

  6. Bob identifies three targeted fixes needed to resolve the zero-balance issue. Watch the Agentic Sidebar as it applies each one.

  7. Bob has applied the fixes to TransactionsPage.js, AccountsPage.js, and BalancesInquiryPage.js.

    • Bob adds token guards and makes the listCustomers API call fault-tolerant.
    • It also requests requests permission to run cd gfm-teller-app && npx react-scripts build to confirm that everything compiles with all three in place.
    • Click Approve for task.

  8. Bob finishes all three fixes. Review the completion message to understand what changed before restarting the app.

  9. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop the running application.

  10. Run npm start to restart the application with the fixes applied.

  11. Return to your browser and sign in again. Your app may look different from the screenshots depending on what Bob generated, and your credentials may differ as well.

  12. The Total Accounts counter now shows 1,000, confirming that the fix worked. Customers and Combined Balances still read zero, which can be revisited later; the portion needed for the module's task is working, so the lab moves forward.

    FOR CLIENT ENGAGEMENTS

    When a demonstration needs every rough edge removed, continue iterating through the same loop — screenshot and plain-language prompt to the Agentic Sidebar — until the remaining counters populate. Module 3 closes with one more example of exactly this.

docs.title: v. COMPLETING THE TELLER TASK
docs.text: The front-end is running and you are signed in. What remains is the task set at the start of the module: find the latest transactions for the client with IBAN DE89545769475769453536.

docs.title: Look up the balance
docs.text:
1. Click Balance Inquiry in the navigation menu to open the IBAN lookup form.

  2. On the Balance Inquiry page, enter the following IBAN into the input field and click Check Balance:

    DE89545769475769453536

  3. The inquiry succeeds and the account details for this IBAN are displayed, confirming that the teller portal is correctly connected to the backend and retrieving live customer data. Recall that this balance (€5,581.33) is the same value the Python teller client returned from the first prompt of this module; it is the balance you should receive on your attempt as well.

docs.title: vi. KEY TAKEAWAYS
docs.text:
• A screenshot and a sentence are a complete bug report for Bob; no knowledge of the root cause is required to start an investigation.
  • Bob verifies before it edits: curl probes against the real backend established the true credentials and the true response shape before any code changed.
  • Read Bob's summary after every fix. It states whether a restart is required and records what changed, which is the trail a regulated environment expects.
  • Restarts remain a human action, and the white screen after one is the React build recompiling rather than a failure.
  • Not every defect must be fixed before moving on; decide which issues block the task at hand and defer the rest deliberately.
  • The balance retrieved through the portal matches the balance the Python client returned, which is the evidence that the generated front-end faithfully reaches the same backend.

The teller portal is built, running, and proven against the live backend. In Module 3 | Secure, Bob turns from builder to reviewer, scanning the GFM Bank codebase for security vulnerabilities and working them through to remediation and verification.

docs.title: Security Analysis and Remediation
docs.text: MODULE 3 | SECURE

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL SECURE
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Secure - Security Analysis and Remediation module for the hands-on enablement. [4 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

This closing module extends Bob's reach to reviewing the code it has been working with all along. The documents it produces — the audit report, the deep dive, and the verification — are the record a regulated environment requires of any change to a system that handles money. Your control remains where it has been throughout. Each fixed file waits for your approval before it is written. The verification report is something you read and judge rather than accept on its word.

The first two modules had Bob understand the GFM Bank system and build on top of it. This module turns Bob into the system's reviewer. You direct it through a vulnerability scan of the codebase, classified against the OWASP Top 10 and CWE. You will afterwards have Bob produce a formal security audit report and a deep dive on the five most critical findings. Finally, Bob will apply the remediations and write a verification report confirming that the fixes have held. A final run of the teller portal confirms that the patches did not break any functionality or systems.

docs.title: ii. WHY THIS MATTERS
docs.text:
Security review is where a regulated industry's expectations are most explicit. A finding is expected to carry a classification and a severity. It must name a location and an attack scenario. It must also propose a remediation and that remediation is expected to be verified rather than assumed. Producing that material by hand is slow work, which is why it so often arrives late, after the code has shipped.

Bob compresses the cycle into a single session. It scans the code and ranks what it finds. It documents the findings and fixes them, then it verifies the result. Each stage is left behind as a file you can hand to an auditor for deeper review and inspection. Whether a finding is accepted, deferred, or challenged remains a judgment left to the human-in-the-loop. This practice mirrors the review-first, trust-later discipline of this entire hands-on lab applied to scenarios where the consequences for failure are highest.

docs.title: iii. SCANNING FOR VULNERABILITIES
docs.text: The scan runs in a fresh session so that Bob's context holds only the security work rather than the state left over from the previous modules.

docs.title: Prepare a clean session
docs.text:
1. Return to IBM Bob and stop any open terminal processes by pressing the Kill (garbage-can) button in the terminal panel.

  2. Press the + button to open a new chat window. A fresh chat gives Bob a clean context window, without the state from Modules 1 and 2, which keeps the security analysis focused.

  3. As a reminder, confirm that you are in Agent mode. If you are comfortable doing so, confirm as well that the Auto-approve permissions are enabled as directed in Module 1.

docs.title: Run the vulnerability scan
docs.text:
1. Paste the following prompt and hit Enter to have Bob perform a comprehensive security vulnerability scan of the codebase:

    Analyze the code files in this project for security vulnerabilities. Identify all security issues, categorize them by type (OWASP Top 10, CWE), and rank them by severity (Critical, High, Medium, Low).

For each vulnerability found, provide:

- Location (file and line number)
- Vulnerability type and category
- Description of the security risk
- Potential attack scenario
- Severity rating with justification

  2. Bob starts working, reading through the Python backend files to identify vulnerabilities and classifying them against the OWASP Top 10 and CWE frameworks.

  3. Bob completes the scan. The analysis may take a minute or two; wait for it to finish before proceeding.

  4. Scroll through the initial portion of Bob's findings and continue reading the full analysis output.

  5. Finish reading the full security analysis. Make a note of the critical and high-severity findings, which are addressed in the sections that follow.

docs.title: iv. DOCUMENTING THE FINDINGS
docs.text: The scan lives in the sidebar. The next two prompts turn it into the documents a review process expects: a structured audit report and a detailed treatment of the most serious findings.

docs.title: Generate the security audit report
docs.text:
1. Paste the following prompt and hit Enter to have Bob generate a structured security audit report:

    Generate a comprehensive SECURITY_AUDIT_REPORT.md document that includes:

 1. **Executive Summary**

    - Overview of files analyzed
    - Total vulnerabilities found by severity
    - Overall risk assessment
    - Key recommendations

 2. **Vulnerability Inventory**
    For each vulnerability:

    - Unique ID (e.g., VULN-001)
    - File and line number
    - Vulnerability title
    - CWE/OWASP classification
    - Severity rating (Critical/High/Medium/Low)
    - CVSS score estimate (if applicable)
    - Detailed description
    - Proof of concept / attack scenario
    - Business impact
    - Remediation recommendation
    - Remediation effort estimate

 3. **Risk Matrix**

    - Visual representation of vulnerabilities by severity and likelihood

 4. **Remediation Roadmap**

    - Prioritized list of fixes
    - Suggested implementation order
    - Dependencies between fixes

 5. **Secure Coding Guidelines**

    - Best practices to prevent similar issues
    - Language-specific recommendations for Python

Save this as SECURITY_AUDIT_REPORT.md in the current directory.

  2. Bob may attempt to generate the entire report in a single pass, which can take several minutes. Wait for the task to complete.

    IF BOB STOPS MID-GENERATION

    If Bob appears to time out or stop part-way through the report, send the prompt continue to resume from where it left off.

  3. When the report is finished, click SECURITY_AUDIT_REPORT.md in the file explorer sidebar to open it.

  4. Right-click the file tab and select Open Preview to view the report with full Markdown formatting applied.

  5. Review SECURITY_AUDIT_REPORT.md. Bob has produced a professional audit document covering every vulnerability found, its severity, and the recommended remediation.

docs.title: Produce the deep dive
docs.text:
1. Paste the following prompt and hit Enter to have Bob produce a detailed treatment of the five most critical vulnerabilities:

    For the top 5 most critical vulnerabilities found, create detailed documentation that includes:

 1. **SQL Injection in data_pipeline.py**

    - Show the vulnerable code
    - Explain why it's vulnerable
    - Demonstrate a potential exploit
    - Show the secure fix using parameterized queries

 2. **Command Injection vulnerabilities**

    - Identify all instances of shell=True
    - Explain the risks
    - Provide secure alternatives using subprocess with lists

 3. **Insecure Deserialization (pickle)**

    - Explain the remote code execution risk
    - Show how an attacker could exploit this
    - Recommend safe alternatives (JSON, safe serialization)

 4. **Hardcoded Secrets**

    - List all hardcoded credentials and secrets
    - Explain the risks of exposure
    - Show how to use environment variables or secret managers

 5. **Cryptographic Weaknesses**

    - Identify weak hashing (MD5) and insecure randomness
    - Explain why these are insufficient for security
    - Provide modern, secure alternatives

  2. Bob starts on the deep-dive documentation, reading the relevant source files and producing detailed exploit scenarios and remediation guidance.

  3. Bob is typically able to complete this in a single pass. When it finishes, VULNERABILITY_DEEP_DIVE.md appears in the project explorer.

  4. Right-click VULNERABILITY_DEEP_DIVE.md and select Open Preview to review the formatted document.

  5. Review the deep dive. Bob has identified real security flaws in the codebase, each with a concrete exploit demonstration and a secure-code fix.

  6. Continue scrolling through the document to read all five vulnerability sections and their recommended fixes.

docs.title: v. REMEDIATING AND VERIFYING
docs.text: With the findings documented, Bob applies the fixes and then reviews its own work. Each fixed file waits for your approval before it is written.

docs.title: Apply the fixes
docs.text:
1. Paste the following prompt and hit Enter to have Bob apply the security fixes to the codebase:

    Fix all security vulnerabilities in the codebase. For each fix:

- Apply the secure coding pattern
- Add comments explaining the security improvement
- Ensure the fix doesn't break existing functionality
- Follow Python security best practices

Specifically:

- Replace string formatting in SQL with parameterized queries
- Replace shell=True with subprocess using argument lists
- Remove or externalize hardcoded credentials
- Replace pickle with JSON for serialization
- Enable SSL verification in requests
- Fix file permissions to restrictive values (0o600)
- Replace MD5 with SHA-256 or bcrypt for password hashing
- Use secrets module instead of random for tokens
- Remove eval/exec or implement strict sandboxing
- Use secure JWT configuration with external secrets

Create the fixed versions of:

- data_pipeline_secure.py

  2. Bob starts applying the fixes. Because it already read the relevant files in the previous prompts, it proceeds directly to the remediation without re-reading the code.

  3. Click Approve for task to allow Bob to write the first fixed file.

  4. Click Approve for task to allow Bob to write the next fixed file.

  5. Click Approve for task to allow Bob to write the final fixed file.

  6. Bob finishes applying the fixes. Review the completion message in the Agentic Sidebar to see what changed in each file.

docs.title: Verify the remediation
docs.text:
1. Paste the following prompt and hit Enter to have Bob verify the fixes and produce a final remediation verification report:

    Review the fixed code files and verify that:

- All identified vulnerabilities have been addressed
- No new security issues have been introduced
- The code still functions correctly
- Security best practices are followed

Generate a REMEDIATION_VERIFICATION.md document that includes:

- Checklist of all vulnerabilities and their fix status
- Any remaining concerns or recommendations
- Suggestions for additional security hardening
- Recommendations for security testing (SAST, DAST, penetration testing)

  2. Bob starts reviewing the fixed files. Click Approve for task when the approval dialog appears.

  3. Click Approve for task to allow Bob to proceed with reading and verifying the fixed files.

  4. Click Approve for task to allow Bob to write the verification report.

  5. Bob confirms that REMEDIATION_VERIFICATION.md has been written to the project directory. Open it to review.

  6. Right-click the file tab and select Open Preview to read the verification report in formatted Markdown.

docs.title: vi. CONFIRMING THE APPLICATION STILL WORKS
docs.text: A remediation that breaks the application is a defect of its own. As a final sanity check, restart the teller portal and confirm that it still runs against the patched backend code.

docs.title: Restart the application
docs.text:
1. If you have lost track of the startup commands after so many prompts, ask Bob in natural language — for example, "How do I start the frontend?" or "What commands do I run to start the GFM teller app?"

  2. Bob understands the question and provides the exact terminal commands needed to start the application again.

  3. Run the startup commands in the terminal to restart the application and confirm that it works correctly after the security fixes.

  4. Sign in again and reach the dashboard. As expected, the application still works.

    WHAT YOU HAVE COMPLETED

    At this point you have completed all three modules of the lab. Because Bob is powered by generative AI, your banking application may look different from the screenshots, and the exact issues you encountered may have varied. What matters is that you have worked the full cycle: codebase analysis in Module 1, a Carbon-based React front-end in Module 2, and vulnerability detection and remediation in Module 3.

docs.title: Optional: apply the remaining polish
docs.text:
For client engagements, or simply for a clean demonstration, the remaining zero-balance counters on the dashboard can be resolved with the same loop used throughout Module 2.

  1. Take a screenshot of the dashboard and send it to Bob with a plain-language description of the problem.

  2. Work through the approval flow in the Agentic Sidebar as usual. Bob investigates the cause, applies the fix, and confirms when it is complete.

  3. Depending on what Bob changed, you may or may not need to restart the development server. If prompted, run npm start in the terminal following the same process used throughout the lab.

  4. Reload the browser and confirm the fix. If the issue is not fully resolved on the first attempt, continue iterating as you have done throughout this lab: take a screenshot and describe the problem, then let Bob work on it.

docs.title: vii. WRAPPING UP
docs.text:
Before concluding, dwell a moment longer on your results and findings across Module 3:

  • A fresh chat session keeps the security analysis focused; context from earlier modules is left behind deliberately.
  • Classifying findings against the OWASP Top 10 and CWE, and ranking them by severity, turns a scan into something a review board can act upon.
  • The three documents — the audit report, the deep dive, and the remediation verification — are the record of the work. Each is a file in the workspace rather than a conversation that scrolls away.
  • Bob applies fixes and then verifies its own work, but each written file passes through your approval and the verification report is yours to judge.
  • Long generations can stall; the prompt continue resumes them.
  • A remediation is complete only once the application has been restarted and proven to work, and the iteration loop remains available for whatever polish a demonstration needs.

Congratulations on reaching the end of the hands-on work and exercises. Across the three modules, Bob has taken GFM Bank from an unfamiliar codebase to a documented, extended, and hardened system.

  • Module 1 produced the written understanding: an architecture reference, a data-pipeline analysis, a functional requirements document, and a catalogue of the invariants the system must never violate.
  • Module 2 turned that understanding into a working Carbon teller portal generated from a single specification. It was then repaired through screenshots and plain-language prompts until it returned the same balance the original Python client did.
  • Module 3 closed the loop with a vulnerability scan classified against the OWASP Top 10 and CWE. That scan became an audit report and a deep dive on the five most critical findings, followed by remediations and a verification report that confirmed the fixes held.

At every one of those stages, you reviewed and approved before anything was trusted. That pairing is the discipline of the AI Maturity Curve exercised on a system that handles money, and it is the story to bring to your next conversation with a client in a regulated industry.

docs.title: viii. EARN ACCREDITATION
docs.text:
In order to receive credit for completion of this course, you must perform one of the two actions (in accordance with your role) described below:

IBMers: RECORD A STAND & DELIVER

IBM regular employees must record a Stand & Deliver to receive credit for this course. By default, IBMers will be evaluated by their First Line Manager (FLM) — although they may request another manager to evaluate their Stand & Deliver, if appropriate. Instructions on how to submit a Stand & Deliver are included within the activity on IBM YourLearning.

Business Partners: COMPLETE THE SKILLS EVALUATION QUIZ

The skills evaluation quiz only applies to business partners. The quiz consists of multiple choice questions, with four possible responses (and only one correct answer) for each question. The quiz questions will ask you about on-screen text or descriptions that come up as you work through the lab guide. Participants must pass the quiz with a grade of 80% or higher. Answers to the quiz can only be determined by carefully following the instructions of the hands-on lab. A link is provided within the course page on IBM Training.

docs.title: Registration and Setup
docs.text: GETTING STARTED

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL CONFIGURE
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Registration and Setup module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

Before beginning Module 1 | Analyze of the hands-on lab, three components must be in place.

PREREQUISITES

  1. The IBM Bob IDE, installed and registered on your local machine.
  2. The lab workspace, downloaded from IBM Seismic and extracted locally.
  3. An authenticated Bob session inside that workspace.

Installation and registration of the Bob IDE are covered in the Setup chapter of Climbing the AI Maturity Curve, which you completed as the prerequisite to this course. This page covers the remaining two components.

docs.title: ii. DOWNLOADING THE LAB WORKSPACE
docs.text: The lab is delivered as a single .zip archive containing the starter project files. Inside are the GFM Bank codebase and the offline Carbon references, along with helper scripts and the pre-configured .bob workspace settings.

docs.title: Download the workspace archive
docs.text:
